name: Virginia

notes: Food for home consumption is taxed at 1%, all of it local; the state's share ended January 1, 2023, and the regional and school sales taxes don't apply to it. Food follows the SNAP definition, so candy and soft drinks are included; hot prepared food, and food from stores whose sales are more than 80% prepared food, are taxed at the full rate.

Alcohol bought in stores: beer, wine and spirits are taxed at the general rate; spirits from Virginia ABC stores also carry a 20% state tax in their price, and wine 40 cents a liter, on top of the sales tax. Neither is counted here: the wine tax is by the liter, and the 20% falls only on spirits, whose share of alcohol bought in stores no official figure gives (liquor stores' national share, used for Mississippi's taxes on package stores, counts wine and beer shops too).

Cigarettes and other tobacco are taxed at the general rate, on top of excise taxes (60 cents a pack, 11 cents a milliliter of vapor liquid, 20% on other tobacco products) and the cigarette taxes many counties and cities levy, which are left out here.
Household supplies: diapers and other incontinence products are taxed at the 1% grocery rate, which is not taken out here.
Personal care products: menstrual products are taxed at the 1% grocery rate, which is not taken out here.
Barber and beauty services: personal services such as haircuts are not taxed.
Clothing is taxed. The yearly sales tax holiday (August 7 to 9 in 2026) exempted clothing and footwear of $100 or less an item, which is not taken out here.
Laundry and dry cleaning: not taxed (FTA 2017 survey answer).

Motor fuel is exempt from the retail sales tax and taxed by the gallon instead: 32.6 cents for gasoline (33.6 for diesel) from July 1, 2026, plus a 9.6-cent motor vehicle fuels sales tax paid by distributors and a 0.2-cent storage tank fee; none is counted here. No 2026 gas tax holiday has been enacted.
Repair and diagnostic labor charged separately is not taxed; parts are.

The general rate is 5.3% (4.3% state, 1% local) and 6% in Northern Virginia, Hampton Roads and Central Virginia (a 0.7% regional tax), 7% in the Historic Triangle (James City County, Williamsburg and York County) and 6.3% in the eight counties and cities with a 1% local sales tax for school construction.

Since 2026 any county or city may add up to 1% for school construction after a referendum (not on groceries or hygiene products). Voters in 47 localities decide on one on November 3, 2026; one approved then can start no sooner than 120 days after its ordinance, so in spring 2027 at the earliest (Code 58.1-605.1; Department of Elections). Each one's page says so; current rates are used here.
Hotel stays pay the sales tax plus local transient occupancy taxes, which are not counted here.
gaps: The state share is 4.3%; the local rate here is the uniform 1% local option plus the regional taxes (0.7% in Northern Virginia, Hampton Roads and Central Virginia; 1% Historic Triangle) and the 1% school construction taxes of eight counties and cities (Charlotte, Gloucester, Halifax, Henry, Northampton, Patrick and Pittsylvania counties and Danville). The regional taxes are state-levied and fund regional transportation or tourism, so they are not strictly city or county revenue.
Groceries and personal hygiene items are taxed at 1% statewide, all of it local.

Virginia's rates are by county and independent city (both are county-level units in Census files); towns take their county's rate, and the towns listed separately are those whose own meals tax is counted.

Local meals taxes are counted in the restaurant rate: every independent city's (the City of Charlottesville's comparison, February 2026) and 71 counties' (each from the county itself). In a town with its own meals tax, the town's rate replaces the county's: 122 towns' rates are counted (each from the town). 15 other towns levy one whose current rate wasn't confirmed from the town (named on their pages); no meals tax is counted in them, since the county's doesn't apply there either. 13 towns list no meals tax of their own, so the county's applies, except in Accomack County, whose tax excludes every incorporated town, and Southampton County, whose tax excludes its six towns by name; 11 more towns there weren't checked for a tax of their own and have none counted. 28 small towns (the largest has about 1,400 people) haven't been checked, or no source was found; their areas take the county's rate (none where the county has none), though nearly every town checked levies its own. 24 counties levy none (Appomattox, Brunswick, Buchanan, Buckingham, Charlotte, Chesterfield, Cumberland, Dickenson, Essex, Giles, Goochland, Grayson, Hanover, Highland, King and Queen, Lancaster, Loudoun, Lunenburg, Mecklenburg, Northumberland, Nottoway, Powhatan, Richmond and Washington; their own pages, budgets or audits and the state auditor's FY2025 report). Lodging, admissions and local cigarette taxes are not counted.

tiers.label: Virginia fiscal stress class
tiers.publisher: Commission on Local Government (Virginia Department of Housing and Community Development)
tiers.what: Ranks Virginia's 133 counties and independent cities by fiscal stress (revenue capacity, revenue effort and median household income) and groups them into four classes, from High to Low stress; local governments and state agencies use it to help allocate state aid (report of November 2025, fiscal year 2023 data).

programs: Business improvement and downtown service districts are mapped for Arlington (Ballston, Rosslyn and National Landing) and Roanoke (Downtown and Williamson Road). Not mapped (no official map found): Richmond's downtown service districts, Norfolk's Downtown Business District, Hampton's Coliseum Central and Downtown Hampton districts, Virginia Beach's Town Center districts (Bayside and Lynn), and the downtown districts of Fairfax City, Franklin, Staunton and Suffolk (all listed in Virginia Tax's 2025 local tax rates report).

Virginia's Tourism Zones (about 75 in 47 localities, set by local ordinance; the Virginia Tourism Corporation's September 2026 map marks each with a numbered point, the newest Halifax County's of May 2026) and Main Street communities have no published boundaries and aren't shown; technology zones and arts and cultural districts are mapped only where a county or city publishes them (Arlington; Richmond, Virginia Beach and Alexandria).

warn.text: Virginia Beach draws many visitors (about $2.6 billion of visitor spending in 2025, by the Virginia Tourism Corporation), but the city as a whole isn't flagged as a visitor economy: its seasonal homes (1.5%) and lodging places per resident (0.5 per 1,000) are spread over a large, mostly residential city, though 9 of its 112 census tracts, the Oceanfront's among them, are flagged on their own. Visitors' spending is part of the city's local sales, so its retention rates likely overstate how much of residents' own spending stays local.

James City County draws many visitors (about $590 million of visitor spending in 2025, by the Virginia Tourism Corporation, around Busch Gardens and Jamestown), but it isn't flagged as a visitor economy: its seasonal homes (3.2%) and lodging places per resident (0.5 per 1,000) fall under the flag's cutoffs, though one of its 17 census tracts is flagged on its own. Visitors' spending is part of its local sales, so its retention rates likely overstate how much of residents' own spending stays local.
